analysis.one_liner: Forces oil companies to pay royalties on old Gulf of Mexico leases when prices are high, before getting new leases.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced March 11, 2025, has no cosponsors and has sat in the House Natural Resources Committee since the day it was introduced, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under leases issued in the late 1990s, some companies drilling in the Gulf of Mexico pay no federal royalties whenever oil and gas prices fall below set thresholds. This bill would require any company that holds one of those leases to renegotiate it so royalties are owed when prices are high, and would bar the Interior Department from giving such a company any new Gulf lease or letting it take over another such lease until it does [S2]. In effect, companies would have to stop getting free production from public waters if they want new access to public waters [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Federal and Gulf-state taxpayers, who receive a share of royalties from oil produced in public waters. When prices rise above the old thresholds, these companies currently pay the government nothing on those leases; the bill would change that, and Americans would get paid for oil taken from waters they own [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Requires companies holding old royalty-relief leases to renegotiate so they owe royalties when oil and gas prices reach the statutory price thresholds, instead of producing royalty-free at any price [S2].
Uses access as leverage: Interior may not issue a new Gulf of Mexico lease, and a covered lease may not be sold or transferred, to any company that has not renegotiated its old leases [S2].
Directs the Interior Secretary to agree to amend leases issued for Central and Western Gulf tracts between 1996 and 2000 to apply the new price thresholds, effective October 1, 2026 [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding legacy Gulf of Mexico leases issued under the Deep Water Royalty Relief Act, which would owe royalties at high prices that they currently do not pay. Some of that cost could reach consumers through fuel prices, though only to the extent companies pass it on [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Gulf deepwater oil and gas producers

drawbacks.text: The bill rewrites the economics of existing contracts after the fact. Companies bid on and paid for those leases under the old royalty-relief terms, and retroactively reopening them could invite years of litigation and make future federal lease sales less attractive to bidders [S2].
Requiring royalty payments raises production costs on those leases, which could modestly increase energy prices or reduce Gulf production if companies pass costs on or scale back output [S2].
Because the bill only conditions new leases and transfers on renegotiation, companies that never seek another Gulf lease or lease transfer could keep their old royalty-free terms untouched [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is public money versus industry margin: companies would pay royalties on oil from public waters that they currently take royalty-free when prices are high, and consumers could see some of that in fuel prices. The design is narrow — it applies only to a defined set of legacy leases and only bites when a company wants new leases or a transfer — so the revenue gain is real but limited, and the retroactive contract change is the strongest argument against it.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and has stayed there, with no cosponsors joining and no committee action taken.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on March 11, 2025 [S1].
It was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote since [S4].
No member of the House — Republican or Democrat — has signed on as a cosponsor [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies holding legacy Gulf of Mexico royalty-relief leases keep producing royalty-free when prices run high, and face no renegotiation pressure, at least for now. Taxpayers are out the royalties they would have collected if the bill had moved [S2].

for.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the Natural Resources Committee, of which he is the senior Democratic member

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 11, 2025 and has taken no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the session to date

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with zero cosponsors it had no path to a vote

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the only supporter in the record is the Democratic sponsor, with zero cosponsors of either party [S3].

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies with legacy Gulf of Mexico deepwater leases
industries.note: These companies hold 1990s-era leases that suspend federal royalties when prices fall below thresholds, letting them produce from public waters royalty-free when prices are high. The bill would end that at the statutory thresholds, redirecting that money to the Treasury — a direct transfer from the companies' margin to public revenue [S2].

industries.industry: Federal and Gulf-coast royalty recipients (Treasury and Gulf state funds)
industries.note: Royalties from offshore drilling are shared with the federal government and Gulf states; requiring payments at high prices would raise this revenue for public use [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action in months, and a divided Congress, this bill is almost certain to die quietly in committee this session, the usual fate for a one-sponsor bill of this kind.
